8.title: "The Beneficent, the Merciful"
8.hook: mercy, named twice, before the word judgment ever appears
8.howItsDone: Muslims say these two names in every unit of every prayer, twice over: in the bismillah and again in verse three. Ar-Rahman and ar-Rahim are also among the names of God Muslims call on in their own prayers, and children are given the names Abdur-Rahman and Abdur-Rahim, servant of the Merciful.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rabb, the one who raises and looks after every world. Your line was every world is tended. Which small world did you notice? Day eight.

A mare stands in a field with her foal pressed close against her legs. She's about to shift her weight, and she stops, lifts one hoof, and holds it in the air, so she won't step on him. A hadith uses exactly that picture. It says that the gentleness creatures show each other, even a mare lifting her hoof from her foal, comes from one small share of a much greater mercy. Today's verse is two words long, and both of them are that mercy.
screen: `A MARE LIFTS HER HOOF.` → `ONE SHARE OF MERCY.` → `VERSE THREE: TWO WORDS.`

segments.voice: Verse three, in Pickthall's words: “The Beneficent, the Merciful.” Ar-Rahman ar-Rahim. If that sounds familiar, it should. They're the two names from verse one, the doorway, said again. Both come from one root, r-h-m, and the noun is today's word: rahma, mercy. The same root makes rahim, the womb. In this language, mercy has the shape of the place where you were held before you were born. A hadith in Bukhari draws the line straight: the ties of the womb, family, kinship, take their name from ar-Rahman. Why two names? One common explanation goes like this. Ar-Rahman is mercy as wide as everything, reaching every creature, whoever they are. Ar-Rahim is mercy that stays, that keeps coming back to you in particular. And the hook's picture? A hadith in Muslim's collection says God made mercy in a hundred parts, and sent one part down into the world. With that one part, creatures are gentle with each other, even the mare lifting her hoof from her foal. The other ninety-nine are kept back. Now look at where the verse sits. Praise, then mercy, then mercy again, and only after that, tomorrow, the word judgment. Some readers see an order in that. Another well-known hadith, in Bukhari and Muslim, says that when God created the world, He wrote that His mercy outstrips His anger. The prayer is built the same way. In the conversation hadith from yesterday, God answers this verse too: My servant has extolled Me. Three verses down, four to go.

segments.voice: The bell will give you about forty-five seconds. Sit comfortably. First, the wide mercy: think of something good that reaches everyone, sunlight, rain, the air in this breath. Stay with it. Then the mercy that stays: someone who kept coming back for you, even when you didn't make it easy. Let their face come. If you pray, you can hold the two names: ar-Rahman, ar-Rahim. If you don't, hold the two pictures. The bell holds the time.
Rahma. Mercy, from the root of the womb, named twice in a row: ar-Rahman, ar-Rahim. Eighth word.
Your line: mercy twice before anything else. Before you judge anything today, a person, a message, yourself, find two kind things to say about it first. Day eight.

9.title: "Owner of the Day of Judgment"
9.hook: a day when every account is settled, held by the one just named merciful
9.carry: the account is in kind hands
9.tomorrow: "Thee (alone) we worship; Thee (alone) we ask for help"
9.howItsDone: Muslims say this verse in every unit of every prayer. Belief in the Last Day is one of the articles of faith in Islam.

segments.voice: Yesterday: rahma, mercy, named twice in a row. Your line was mercy twice before anything else. Did you find two kind things to say before you judged something? Day nine.

A shopkeeper's ledger has two columns: what came in, and what went out. Most of a life never makes it into a ledger. Dishes washed that weren't yours. An angry text deleted before it was sent. A night spent sitting up with someone, never mentioned again. Nobody writes the quiet stuff down. And on the other side, the things nobody caught. Today's verse says both columns are kept. Dropped into the middle of a prayer about mercy, that can sound like a warning. Listen to where it sits.
screen: `A LEDGER WITH TWO COLUMNS.` → `THE GOOD NOBODY WROTE DOWN.` → `BOTH COLUMNS ARE KEPT.`

segments.voice: Verse four, in Pickthall's words: “Owner of the Day of Judgment.” In Arabic, maliki yawmi d-din. Today's word is the day itself: yawm ad-din. Yawm is day. And din, translated judgment, is also the everyday Arabic word for religion, a way of life. At its root it carries the sense of a debt coming due, an account settled. So this is the day when every account is squared, both columns, the unseen good and the unfinished wrong. Two details for the curious. The Qur'an has more than one accepted way of being recited, and in some that first word is maalik, owner, the reading Pickthall translates. In others it's malik, king. Both are accepted. Now, where it sits. Two verses of praise and mercy, the Beneficent, the Merciful, and only then the Day. The same one who was just named merciful, twice, is the one who holds the account. Some readers take that order as the point: the reckoning isn't in the hands of a stranger, or an enemy, or a machine. It's held by mercy. And in that reading, the Day promises that nothing quiet is lost: the dishes, the unsent message, the night beside someone. In the conversation hadith recorded by Muslim, God answers this verse too: My servant has glorified Me. Some narrations add: My servant has entrusted his affairs to Me. Read that way, the verse isn't dread. It's handing the account over. Four verses down, three to go. And tomorrow, the prayer turns around.

segments.voice: The bell will give you about forty-five seconds. Think of one good thing you did that nobody noticed. Let it be small. Hold it, and let it be enough that it happened. Then think of one thing you'd like to settle well, an apology, a debt, a promise. Don't solve it. Just set it down in front of you, honestly. If you pray, you can let the Arabic sit with both: maliki yawmi d-din. The bell holds the time.
Yawm ad-din. The Day of Judgment, the day every account is settled, held by the one just named merciful. Ninth word.
Your line: the account is in kind hands. Today, do one good thing nobody will see, and don't mention it to anyone. Day nine.

10.title: "Thee (alone) we worship; Thee (alone) we ask for help"
10.hook: the hinge of the prayer: it turns from talking about God to talking to God, and it says one
10.howItsDone: Muslims say this verse in every unit of every prayer. Tawhid is the heart of Muslim belief, said in the shahada, and many Muslims raise the index finger of the right hand when they bear witness in the sitting part of the prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday: yawm ad-din, the day every account is settled. Your line was the account is in kind hands. Did you manage one good thing nobody saw? Day ten.
screen: `YAWM AD-DIN — THE ACCOUNT, HELD BY MERCY.`

segments.voice: Mecca, in the early years. A man named Bilal is enslaved there, and he has become a Muslim. The early biographies say the man who owned him would drag him out into the noon heat, lay him on the burning sand, put a heavy rock on his chest, and tell him to give up his new faith. And Bilal, crushed under the stone, would say only one word, over and over. Ahad. Ahad. One. One. He'll come back later on this path, as the voice of the call to prayer. Today, his word, and the verse where al-Fatiha says it.

Verse five, in Pickthall's words: “Thee (alone) we worship; Thee (alone) we ask for help.” In Arabic, iyyaka na'budu wa iyyaka nasta'in. Two things happen here. First, the prayer turns around. For four verses it has talked about God: praise be to Him, the Merciful, the Owner of the Day. Now, suddenly, it talks to God. You. In the conversation hadith recorded by Muslim, God's answer changes here too: this is between Me and My servant, and My servant shall have what he asked. Second, listen to the order of the Arabic. It doesn't say we worship You. It says You, we worship. Putting You first makes it exclusive. Pickthall marks that by adding the word alone, in brackets. Only You. And only You for help. That little word, alone, is today's word in miniature. Tawhid. The root is w-h-d, one; wahid is the number one. Tawhid is a word of action: making one, affirming one. It's the first half of the shahada you met with the pillars: there is no god but God. It has its own surah, four lines long. In Pickthall's words: “Say: He is Allah, the One!” That's surah one hundred and twelve, al-Ikhlas, sincerity, and a hadith in Bukhari says it's equal to a third of the Qur'an. Here's why it matters on an ordinary Tuesday. If God is one, everything else, however big it looms, isn't God. Your job, your phone, your fear, other people's opinion of you: real, none of them ultimate. One way to put tawhid: living with one center instead of a dozen. That's what Bilal was saying under the rock. Not an argument. The center, holding. Five verses down, two to go.
screen: `THE PRAYER TURNS: ABOUT GOD, TO GOD.` · `YOU, WE WORSHIP — YOU ALONE.` · `W-H-D — ONE.` · `ONE CENTER, NOT A DOZEN.` · then, large: `ONE.`

segments.voice: The bell will give you about forty-five seconds. Sit still, and gather your attention into one place: the breath at the tip of your nose. Just that. When your mind splits off into a dozen places, the list, the text, the worry, notice it, and bring it back to the one breath. Again and again. In the prayer, at the words of witness, it's common to raise one finger of the right hand; you can rest one finger up while you sit, if you like. If you pray, let the word rest there: ahad. The bell holds the time.
Tawhid. The oneness of God, affirmed: You alone we worship, You alone we ask for help. Tenth word.
Your line: one. Today, when you catch yourself pulled in a dozen directions, pick one thing, and do only that for five minutes. Day ten.

11.title: "Show us the straight path"
11.hook: the whole prayer is a request for directions
11.tomorrow: "The path of those whom Thou hast favoured; Not (the path) of those who earn Thine anger nor of those who go astray"
11.howItsDone: Muslims ask for the straight path in every unit of every prayer, at least seventeen times a day. Many also use the phrase in their own prayers and conversations, asking to be guided in a decision.

segments.voice: Yesterday: tawhid, the oneness of God, and the verse where the prayer turns to say You alone. Your line was simply one. Did you give five minutes to one thing? Day eleven.

Think about the last time you were properly lost. Not a little turned around. Lost. The phone at two percent, the street signs in a language you don't read, every corner looking like the one before. What did you finally do? You stopped someone and asked. Which way? It's a humbling question. It admits you don't know. Here's the surprise at the center of the prayer Muslims say most. Five verses of praise and mercy and trust, and then, when it finally asks for something, it doesn't ask for money, or health, or even forgiveness. It asks for directions.
screen: `PROPERLY LOST.` → `WHICH WAY?` → `THE PRAYER ASKS FOR DIRECTIONS.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the prayer said: You alone we ask for help. Today it asks. Verse six, in Pickthall's words: “Show us the straight path.” In Arabic, ihdina s-sirata l-mustaqim. Take it one word at a time. Ihdina: show us, guide us. It comes from the root h-d-y, guidance, the same root as hidaya, guidance, and as hadiya, a gift. Guidance, in this language, is something handed to you. Sirat is a road, a wide, clear way. And mustaqim: straight, standing upright, not bending. Put the last two together and you have today's word, as-sirat al-mustaqim, the straight path. Notice the small word: us. Even someone praying completely alone, at three in the morning, says show us. Nobody asks for the road just for themselves. In the conversation hadith recorded by Muslim, God answers this last part of the prayer: this is for My servant, and My servant shall have what he asked. And one more surprise. Muslims who pray the five prayers ask for this at least seventeen times a day. Even people who've prayed for fifty years. Why keep asking for a road you're already on? Scholars give a simple answer: the path isn't found once. You ask to be shown it, and to be kept on it, again at every corner. It's less like a map you memorize and more like a friend walking beside you, pointing, turn after turn. Six verses down, one to go.
screen: `IHDINA — SHOW US, A GIFT.` · `SIRAT — A WIDE, CLEAR ROAD.` · `MUSTAQIM — STRAIGHT, UPRIGHT.` · `ASKED AGAIN AT EVERY CORNER.` · then, large: `SHOW US THE WAY.`

segments.voice: The bell will give you about forty-five seconds. Sit comfortably. Think of one place in your life where you honestly don't know which way to go. A decision, a relationship, a next step. Don't solve it. Just stand at that corner for a moment and admit you don't know. If you pray, you can carry the line in Arabic or English: show us the straight path. If you don't, just hold the question open, like a hand. The bell holds the time.
As-sirat al-mustaqim. The straight path: the road al-Fatiha asks to be shown, seventeen times a day. Eleventh word.
Your line: show us the way. Today, ask someone for directions you'd usually pretend you don't need. A coworker, a friend, a map. Notice how it feels to ask. Day eleven.

12.title: "The path of those whom Thou hast favoured; Not (the path) of those who earn Thine anger nor of those who go astray"
12.hook: the road described by the people on it, and the word said when the prayer ends
12.carry: walk with the ones who walked it well
12.howItsDone: Muslims recite this verse to close al-Fatiha in every unit of every prayer. In congregation, Sunni Muslims then say amin together, aloud or quietly depending on the school; Shia Muslims of the Ja'fari school do not say amin in the prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday: as-sirat al-mustaqim, the straight path, asked for seventeen times a day. Your line was show us the way. Did you ask anyone for directions? Day twelve.

Fresh snow on a mountain trail, and not a sign anywhere. But a line of boot prints runs up ahead, deep and steady, left by people who came through this morning. Nobody needs a map up here. You put your feet where theirs went. Yesterday al-Fatiha asked to be shown the straight path. Today, in its last verse, it says what that path looks like, and it does it the same way: not with a map, but with the people already on it.
screen: `BOOT PRINTS IN FRESH SNOW.` → `FOLLOW THE ONES ALREADY ON IT.` → `VERSE SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Verse seven, in Pickthall's words: “The path of those whom Thou hast favoured; Not (the path) of those who earn Thine anger nor of those who go astray.” It answers yesterday's request. Which path? The one walked by those God has favored. Another verse of the Qur'an names who they are: the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs, the righteous, and it calls them the best of company. So the straight path isn't an abstract rule. It's a road with footprints on it. Then the verse names two ways of missing it: those who earn anger, and those who go astray. Commentators have read those two in more than one way. One common reading hears two kinds of lost: knowing the way and walking off it, and never finding it at all. The prayer asks to be kept from both. And then, all seven verses said, comes one more word, not part of the surah itself. Amin. It means, roughly: O God, answer this. Accept it. Jews and Christians say it too, as amen. A hadith in Bukhari says that when the one leading the prayer reaches the last words, those praying behind should say amin, because the angels say amin with them, and whoever's amin matches the angels' is forgiven what came before. In Sunni practice it's said after al-Fatiha in prayer, aloud in some schools and quietly in others; Shia Muslims of the Ja'fari school don't say it in the prayer. That's the whole opening. A name, praise, mercy twice, the Day, You alone, the road, and the people on it. Seven verses, and you've walked every one.

segments.voice: The bell will give you about forty-five seconds. Think of one person who walked a hard road well. Someone in your family, a teacher, a neighbor, someone you've only read about. Picture them clearly: their face, the way they carried themselves. Ask yourself one thing: what did they do that you'd like to do too? Let the answer be small. If you pray, you can end the minute with one quiet word: amin. The bell holds the time.
Amin. O God, answer this: the word said when al-Fatiha ends, the seven verses complete. Twelfth word.
Your line: walk with the ones who walked it well. Today, do one thing the way that person you pictured would have done it. Day twelve.

13.title: washing before prayer
13.hook: washing before prayer; water as a reset
13.howItsDone: Muslims make wudu before each prayer unless they are still in a state of wudu from an earlier washing; mosques have washing areas with taps, and at home it's done at an ordinary sink.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the last verse of al-Fatiha, and a single word said when it ends: amin. Your line was walk with the ones who walked it well. Who came to mind? Day thirteen.
screen: `AMIN — WALK WITH THE ONES WHO WALKED IT WELL.`

segments.voice: Near the door of a mosque there's often a room of water: a row of taps along a wall, a low ledge or a line of stools to sit on, a drain running along the floor. Before the prayer, people stop here first. Sleeves pushed up, shoes off. Water over the hands, into the mouth, over the face, up the arms, over the feet. Nobody is rushing. This isn't about dirt; the washing is for something else. It's the step between the street and the prayer. Today: the water that comes before the words.
screen: `A ROW OF TAPS BY THE DOOR.` → `HANDS, MOUTH, FACE, ARMS, FEET.` → `WATER BEFORE THE WORDS.`

segments.voice: The word is wudu. Its root, w-d-a, carries the sense of brightness and clean light: the same root gives words for a shining face. The Qur'an sets it out in one verse, in Pickthall's words: “When ye rise up for prayer, wash your faces, and your hands up to the elbows.” Then the head is lightly wiped, and the feet. That's the core. Over time the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ showed his companions the whole shape, and it's the shape Muslims use today. In the common Sunni form, it begins with an intention, often with bismillah. Then the hands, three times. Water in the mouth, and the nose. The face, from hairline to chin, ear to ear. Each arm to the elbow. A wet hand over the head, and the ears. The feet. The clearest difference comes here, and both sides read the same verse. Sunni Muslims wash the feet. Shia Muslims wipe them with a wet hand. What's it for? A hadith in Muslim's collection pictures it this way: as the water runs off the face, the wrongs the eyes have looked at run off with it; off the hands, what the hands did; off the feet, where the feet went. Another says cleanliness is half of faith. So wudu isn't only hygiene. It's a reset, done with the body, before speaking to God. And if there's no water, in a desert, or when water would harm you, the same verse allows tayammum: touching clean earth and wiping the face and hands. The reset is never out of reach. The day doesn't have to come with you into the prayer.
screen: `WUDU — FROM A ROOT OF BRIGHTNESS.` · `HANDS, MOUTH, FACE, ARMS, HEAD, FEET.` · `THE WRONGS RUN OFF WITH THE WATER.` · `NO WATER? CLEAN EARTH.` · then, large: `WASH YOUR FACES.`

segments.voice: The bell will give you about forty-five seconds. If there's water nearby, go and wash your hands slowly, and feel it run off your fingers. If there isn't, rest your hands open on your knees and picture cool water running over them, then your face. Either way, choose one thing from today you'd like to rinse off. A sharp word, a worry, a scroll you regret. Let the water take it. The bell holds the time.
Wudu. The washing before prayer: hands, mouth, face, arms, head and feet. A reset with water. Thirteenth word.
Your line: rinse the day off. Tonight, when you wash your face, do it slowly, and let one thing from today go down the drain with the water. Day thirteen.

14.title: why five times
14.hook: why five times; standing, bowing, forehead to the ground
14.tomorrow: the call to prayer, and why it's beautiful
14.howItsDone: Muslims pray salat five times a day, facing Mecca, in a set sequence of standing, bowing, prostrating and sitting; they may pray at home, at work, at a mosque, or anywhere clean.

segments.voice: Yesterday: wudu, the washing before prayer. Your line was rinse the day off. Did the water take anything with it? Day fourteen.

Ten past one on a weekday, in the stockroom behind a hardware store. One of the staff flattens a clean cardboard box on the floor, turns to face a particular direction, and stands very still. Then he bows, hands on his knees. Then he goes all the way down, forehead to the cardboard, between the paint cans and the delivery crates. A few minutes later he folds the box away and goes back to the register. Why five times a day? And why the whole body? Today's word is the prayer itself.
screen: `A STOCKROOM, JUST AFTER ONE.` → `FOREHEAD TO THE FLOOR.` → `WHY FIVE? WHY THE BODY?`

segments.voice: Salat. It's the second of the five pillars, and it isn't quite what English means by prayer. Du'a is asking, in your own words, any time. Salat is a set shape, at set times, with set words. Pickthall often translates it as worship: “Lo! worship preserveth from lewdness and iniquity.” The five times follow the sun. Fajr before sunrise. Dhuhr after midday. Asr in the afternoon. Maghrib just after sunset. Isha at night. Where does five come from? A hadith in Bukhari tells it. On the Night Journey, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ was given fifty daily prayers. On the way back, Musa, Moses, asked him what he'd been given, and said: your people can't manage that, go back and ask for less. He went back, again and again, until it was five. And God said: five, with the reward of fifty. In Sunni practice they're usually prayed at five separate times. Shia practice allows the same five prayers to be joined into three sittings: noon with afternoon, sunset with night. Now the body. Each prayer is made of units called rak'ahs, and each unit moves through the same shapes. Standing, and reciting al-Fatiha, the seven verses you've just walked through. Bowing, back flat, hands on the knees. Standing again. Then sujud: forehead, nose, palms, knees and toes on the ground. A hadith in Muslim's collection says a person is never nearer to God than in that position. The highest part of you, the part that thinks, set down where your feet were. The body isn't just carried along to the prayer. It's saying something the words can't.
screen: `SALAT — A SET SHAPE, AT SET TIMES.` · `FIVE TIMES, FOLLOWING THE SUN.` · `FIFTY, THEN FIVE.` · `STANDING, BOWING, FOREHEAD DOWN.` · then, large: `NEVER NEARER THAN IN SUJUD.`

segments.voice: The bell will give you about forty-five seconds. If you're able, stand for a moment, then bow a little, hands on your knees, and notice how your breath changes in each shape. If you'd rather stay seated, just lower your head toward your chest, slowly, and feel what the body says when it bows. Stay there. Let the body do the praying for once, without any words. The bell holds the time.
Salat. The prayer in its set shape: five times a day, standing, bowing, forehead to the ground. Fourteenth word, and two weeks on your strand.
Your line: the body prays too. Once today, notice your posture at a hard moment, and change it. Stand up straight, or bow your head, or just open your hands. Two weeks, done. Day fourteen.
